title: Connector erasure: three permanent failures present as retryable and nothing dead-letters; the unresolvable path records no deletion log (Peter F6/F9)
description:
**BLUF — on the connector erasure path three PERMANENT failure causes are answered as if they were retryable, and nothing dead-letters. Platform S retries without bound, so two of the three spin forever. Found by Peter reviewing #790 (F6), with F9 folded in as the same class.**

The whole design of `POST /api/gdpr/erasures` is built around never stranding a retry — it deliberately never 404s, because a non-terminal answer against an unbounded retry strands an Art. 17 obligation. The mirror-image case was left open.

### F6 — permanent failures wearing a retryable face

Peter's table, verified on the tree:

| cause | response | can a retry ever succeed? |
| -- | -- | -- |
| connector key with no tenant (`validateApiKey` defaults `tenantId: ''`, so the claim is omitted) | 403 | **no** |
| non-uuid `tenantId` claim → 22P02 | 500 | **no** |
| genuine step failure inside `executeErasureImpl` | 500 | yes |

The first two are configuration faults on the key. S cannot fix them by retrying and there is nothing to move the request into, so it spins.

### F9 — the unresolvable path records nothing

`executeErasureByExternalRef`'s unresolvable branch blanks provenance identity columns and returns, writing **no** `data_deletion_log` **row**; the never-seen branch logs nothing at all. So the one branch that most needs an audit trail — K erased something for a subject it holds no user row for — leaves no record that it ran.

### Why one ticket

Both are about what this path records when it does *not* take the happy route: F6 is the request that can never succeed and is never parked; F9 is the erasure that succeeds and is never recorded. A dead-letter design wants to answer both at once.

### Not fixed in #790

A dead-letter path is a design, not a line, and #790 was already carrying four Majors. Recorded here rather than folded in silently.

Found: Peter, review of PR #790, 2026-09-02 12:46Z (F6, F9). Verified 2026-09-02 (session 110) on `feature/ks-695-ask1-erasure-by-external-ref` at `941ea960a`.

nodes.title: Refs KS-758 F9: the unresolvable connector erasure records its deletion log

nodes.body:
**F9's half is on `develop`. PR #1666 merged as `21e0c39149ca22e623835e07691c032dd6550f91`, tree `f35c24a340f639f588900bcc6e6cde9fbaba88e9`, one parent `88933d5c7ebb`. The F6 half — three permanent failures presenting as retryable, and the dead-letter design — is untouched, so this stays open.**

**What landed.** The unresolvable connector-erasure branch now writes a `data_deletion_log` row, with `data_type 'action_provenance'` and `deletion_method 'anonymize'` — the pair the resolved path already uses, so migration 036's CHECK cannot reject it (that migration exists because a CHECK violation on this table once aborted an erasure *after* the subject's DEK was destroyed). `user_id` and `dsr_id` are NULL by construction, so the INSERT omits them. The never-seen branch gets a log line with a `cause` field and **no row**: nothing was changed there, and a deletion-log entry for a no-op would assert an erasure that did not happen.

**`reason` keeps a one-way keyed hash of the reference — option (c), which Kam ruled at 14:01:14 AEDT.** Round 1 built (b), the card's default while it was open; (b)'s exact string is now the **fallback** when the lookup key is unregistered, logged as a warn carrying no reference, because the blanking has already irreversibly happened and the erasure must still succeed.

The hash is `lookupHash` — HMAC-SHA256 on a 32-byte `PII_LOOKUP_HMAC_KEY`, separate from the encryption KEK but **the same key and construction as `users.email_lookup_hash`**, so one compromise reaches both. It is computed on the reference as the service receives it: both request paths trim it through `ExternalRefSchema` (`routes/gdpr.ts:514`), nothing lowercases it anywhere, and all four comparisons in this file are raw equality on that same value.

⚠ **What a reader learns, stated rather than glossed.** With the key, recomputing the hash for a subject you can already name **proves that person was erased** — the capability (c) exists to keep. Without it, the hash is deterministic and **unsalted**, so a reader who can **anchor** one hash to a reference they already hold identifies that subject; and via the cross-tenant deletion-log read (**KS-1696**) that reader can be another organisation's admin, since the hash carries no tenant. So **(c) replaces a plaintext identifier with a deterministic, unsalted, anchorable one plus a correlator** — better than (a), **not equivalent to** (b).

**Eleven cells over two rounds, red-proved across seven arms each**, with the pre-existing cells inside the judged set so collateral counts as failure; every arm `tsc --noEmit` rc 0 before running, and the product restored by sha256 equality after each. Three of round 2's cells close test gaps **gate CE1 found in my own round 1**: a case-sensitive no-raw-ref check, a hard-codeable `records_affected`, and two `cause` labels that could be swapped undetected.

**Suite:** `135 suites / 1576 → 1587 tests, 0 failed` — **+11, 0 vanished**. Type-checked by hand, because `services/originate` has no `tsconfig.test.json` and is outside preflight leg 16 (recorded on KS-1090).

**Known residue** (in the PR body, including six notes gate CL1 raised against work it approved): raw hashing is pinned by no test; the warn test checks only the exact-case reference; the no-catch arm fails by a throw rather than an assertion; a missing key gives **no startup signal** — compose and bicep wire the variable but neither guarantees a value, so in such a deployment (c) silently degrades to (b); three log lines still carry the reference, as Kam's ruling allows; and concurrent requests could write two rows.

**Round 2: Kam ruled option (c) at 14:01:14 AEDT, so the `reason` now keeps a one-way KEYED hash of the reference rather than a bare category. PR #1666 is at head `d8e8e65b816a6fe7a469d2955e33ce0c040d15f5` (a fast-forward over round 1's `b5d65c8e0651`). Round 1 built (b), which was the card's default while it was still open — (b)'s exact string survives as the fallback.**

```
GDPR erasure request (connector — unresolved subject, provenance identity blanked; ref_hmac=<64 hex>)
```

`lookupHash` is **HMAC-SHA256 over a 32-byte `PII_LOOKUP_HMAC_KEY`**, a key deliberately separate from the encryption KEK. A bare SHA-256 was never an option and `encryptedField.ts:567-571` already argues why: an attacker with offline access can brute-force a small search space, which a Platform-S PersonGuid is.

**The ref is hashed raw**, because `external_ref` is normalised nowhere in this file — all four comparisons are raw SQL equality — unlike email, which every other caller lowercases and trims. Two case-variant refs therefore hash differently; that is already true of the lookup.

**A missing key degrades rather than fails.** `lookupHash` throws when unregistered, and the blanking has already irreversibly happened, so the reason falls back to (b)'s category and a warn carrying **no reference** is logged. The state is reachable: `initFromEnv` registers only `if (hmacKey)`, compose passes `${PII_LOOKUP_HMAC_KEY:-}` and bicep a `secretRef` — neither guarantees a non-empty value. In such a deployment **(c) silently degrades to (b)**. *Not measured: whether the live vault holds a non-empty key — that needs Azure access.*

⚠ **The honest cost of (c), recorded rather than glossed:** with the key, recomputing the hash for a subject you can already name **proves that person was erased** — the capability (c) keeps. Without the key, nothing about *which* subject, but **two rows with the same hash are the same subject**, so an unprivileged reader can count distinct erased subjects and see repeats. **(c) removes the identifier and keeps a correlator.** Against KS-1696's cross-tenant read that is better than (a) and worse than (b).

**Five cells, three of which close gaps gate CE1 found in my own round 1:** H1 (the hash of the raw ref, no raw ref), H2 (key unregistered → bare category, erasure still completes, warn with no reference), H3 (64 hex, ref absent **case-insensitively** — CE1: round 1's check was case-sensitive), G-a (`records_affected` is the UPDATE's own count; the fixture now returns 7, so hard-coding 1 fails), G-c (each `cause` label asserted against its own branch, so swapping them reds).

**Red-proof: 7 arms over 11 cells** — round 2's five plus round 1's six, so collateral is judged and none appeared. Notably **option (a) written back in reds H1, H3, F2 and FC1**. Each arm `tsc` rc 0 first; product restored by sha256 equality.

**Suite:** `135 suites / 1582 → 1587 tests, 0 failed` — +5, 0 vanished on top of round 1's +6. Hand type-check 0 errors across 157 test files, because originate is outside preflight leg 16.

Still `Refs` — KS-758's F6 half (the retryable-looking permanent failures and the dead-letter design) is untouched.

**F9's half is built. PR #1666 is up at head `b5d65c8e0651a780fd594f4859d1f6282256d051` — the unresolvable connector-erasure branch now records a `data_deletion_log` row, with a bare category `reason` and no subject reference. The F6 half (permanent failures wearing a retryable face, and the dead-letter design) is untouched, so this is `Refs` and the ticket stays open.**

**The two unresolvable branches get deliberately different treatment:**

| branch | data | now records |
|---|---|---|
| provenance rows still carry identity | **blanked** for the ref | a `data_deletion_log` row **and** the pre-existing `logger.info` |
| ref never seen, or already blanked | **nothing changed** | a `logger.info` with a `cause` field, and **no row** |

The second gets no row on purpose: nothing was changed there, and a deletion-log entry for a no-op would assert an erasure that did not happen in the table that *is* the Art. 17 accountability record. The log line separates `ref-never-seen` from `already-erased`, which the response cannot — both answer `completed / alreadyErased: true`.

**`data_type` `'action_provenance'` and `deletion_method` `'anonymize'`** are the same pair the resolved path already uses for this table, so migration 036's CHECK cannot reject the row. That matters because 036 exists after a CHECK violation on this very table aborted an erasure *after* the subject's DEK was destroyed (KS-291). `user_id` and `dsr_id` are NULL by construction, so the INSERT uses the column list that omits them.

**Why `reason` carries no `external_ref` — measured, not stylistic.** Kam's card `secuura-ks758-erasure-log-subject-ref-1020` read `status open, choice=None` at 2026-10-20 13:3x AEDT, and its default is option (b). A reader census run two ways says the same thing: by column there are only 4 non-test references to the table, but **by mapping** `mapDeletionLogRow` copies `reason` verbatim into `DeletionLogEntry`, which reaches HTTP at three places and is in the OpenAPI contract. `GET /api/gdpr/deletion-log` admits `ORG_ADMIN` and, with no `userId`, runs an unfiltered `SELECT` over a table with **no `tenant_id` column and no RLS policy**. An `external_ref` written into `reason` would be a Platform-S subject reference readable by another organisation's admin. **That read is a separate defect, filed as KS-1696 (Bug, High), and is not addressed here.**

**The write is fail-soft.** The blanking has already happened and is irreversible; throwing would answer 5xx for an erasure that *did* complete, to a caller that retries without bound — this ticket's own F6 spin. A failure is logged at `error` and the erasure still reports `completed`. Cell F4 pins it.

**Six cells, red-proof complete over 7 arms**, each `tsc --noEmit` rc 0 before anything ran, product restored by sha256 equality after each, comparator self-tested four ways:

| arm | my failing cells |
|---|---|
| no mutation (positive control) | none, **46/46** |
| the INSERT removed (pre-fix product) | F1 F2 F3 F4 FC1 |
| **option (a) — `external_ref` in `reason`** | **F2, FC1** |
| `user_id`/`dsr_id` named in the column list | F1 F2 F3 |
| fail-soft removed | F4 |
| a row written on the never-seen branch | F5 |
| `data_type` outside the existing vocabulary | F1 |

Whole originate suite `135 suites / 1576 → 1582 tests, 0 failed`, rc 0 — **+6, 0 vanished**.

⚠ **Two things a reviewer should know.** `services/originate` has no `tsconfig.test.json` and is outside preflight leg 16's corpus — this PR's push printed `typecheck-tests` for auth, api-gateway and vc-issuer and **no originate line** — so nothing at the gate type-checks this PR's test file; I ran it by hand (157 test files in the program, 0 errors) and the gap is recorded on KS-1090. And cells F1/F2 read bound values **positionally**, so a future legitimate column-list change reds three cells rather than one.

If (a) or (c) is ruled before this merges it is a one-line change plus its cells — (c) additionally needs `lookupHash`'s throw path covered, since it throws when `PII_LOOKUP_HMAC_KEY` is unregistered and the erasure must still succeed.

## The two gdpr erasure endpoints came off the schemathesis failing set — measured, not fixed here

`GET /api/gdpr/erasures/{externalRef}` and `POST /api/gdpr/erasures` failed in **every** pre-rebuild run (s152 12:12Z, and two more at 12:57Z / 13:00Z) and passed in **every** post-rebuild run (13:05Z / 13:07Z), on the same commit `5ffaaf396` — so the fix was already in the code and a stale local image was hiding it.

⚠ **This does NOT say this ticket is done.** The measurement separates old code from new code, not one commit from another, and the erasure family spans KS-695 / KS-754 / KS-757 / KS-758. Attributing the change to any one of them needs a bisect that was not run.

Full cells and controls on **KS-695**. *(s153, 2026-09-08.)*
